note.text: Hair is protein, so when a client tells me her strands feel weaker and thinner, the building blocks are one of the first places I look. I'd rather see what your scalp and your history are telling us than hand you another powder to try. The good news is that once we know what's missing, follicles are remarkably willing to respond.

shortAnswer.text: Amino acids are the building blocks the body uses to make hair. They support keratin, follicle structure, scalp circulation, collagen, and pathways that influence the growth cycle. More protein is not automatically the answer. The useful question is whether your history, scalp pattern, and focused testing point to a specific gap rather than another generic supplement.
takeaways: Use the scalp read to narrow the question.

body.toc: Why a list is not a plan
body.text: Why a list is not a plan

It is tempting to turn amino acids into another shopping list. That misses the point. Hair depends on building blocks, but the useful question is not which ingredient is popular. It is which part of your own picture is asking for support.

Lysine and methionine already give us two different examples. One can point us toward an iron story, while the other can point toward sulfur. Those are not interchangeable questions, and neither can be settled by taking more of everything.
The goal is not the longest supplement label. It is a plan that can explain why each ingredient is there.

We begin with the pattern at the scalp, the timing of the shedding, what you eat, what you already take, and what changed before the hair changed. That history helps separate a possible building-block issue from a scalp condition or another internal driver.

body.text: Only after those pieces agree does a targeted nutrient plan make sense. If they point somewhere else, adding amino acids is not the answer, and we will say so.
What progress should mean
A useful plan gives you something clearer than hope in a bottle. You should understand what is being supported, why it belongs in your plan, and what will be reviewed over time.
Hair changes slowly, so the first win is often clarity. Once the guessing stops, each next decision becomes easier and more personal.

faq.q: Do amino acids help hair grow?
faq.a: They are part of the raw material the body uses to make hair, but that does not mean every amino acid supplement fits every shedding pattern. The useful next step is to connect the scalp, history, food, current supplements, and any focused testing before choosing support.

faq.q: Why might more protein not fix shedding?
faq.a: Eating more protein does not tell us which building block may be relevant, whether it is being used well, or whether the hair change has another cause. A scalp condition, stress pathway, iron question, or different internal driver may need attention instead.

faq.q: Which amino acids belong in a hair plan?
faq.a: That decision should be personal. This article discusses lysine in relation to iron and methionine in relation to sulfur, but it does not prescribe a universal list. Dr. Nina uses the scalp pattern, history, and focused results to decide whether either question belongs in the plan.

faq.q: Should I take a general hair vitamin?
faq.a: A general vitamin may add ingredients without explaining which one you need. A better plan can tell you why each recommendation is present, what question it addresses, and when it will be reviewed. If the evidence points elsewhere, more supplements are not the answer.
